Microlocal decoupling inequalities and the distance problem on Riemannian manifolds

Alex Iosevich Address: Department of Mathematics, University of Rochester, Rochester NY, 14620 Email address: alex.iosevich@rochester.edu , Bochen Liu Address: Department of Mathematics & International Center for Mathematics, Southern University of Science and Technology, Shenzhen 518055, China Email address: Bochen.Liu1989@gmail.com and Yakun Xi Address: School of Mathematical Sciences, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou 310027, PR China Email address: yakunxi@zju.edu.cn
Abstract.

We study the generalization of the Falconer distance problem to the Riemannian setting. In particular, we extend the result of Guth–Iosevich–Ou–Wang for the distance set in the plane to general Riemannian surfaces. Key new ingredients include a family of refined microlocal decoupling inequalities, which are related to the work of Beltran–Hickman–Sogge on Wolff-type inequalities, and an analog of Orponen’s radial projection lemma which has proved quite useful in recent work on distance sets.

1. Introduction

The Falconer distance problem has been a central and persistently difficult question in harmonic analysis and geometric measure theory since 1986 when it was introduced by Falconer [Fal86]. He conjectured that if the Hausdorff dimension of a compact subset E⊂ℝdE\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d}, d≥2d\geq 2, is greater than d2\frac{d}{2}, then the Lebesgue measure of the distance set,

Δ(E)={|x−y|:x,y∈E}\Delta(E)=\{|x-y|:x,y\in E\}

is positive, where |⋅||{}\cdot{}| denotes the Euclidean distance. Considering a suitably thickened and scaled integer lattice shows that the exponent d2\frac{d}{2} would be best possible.

Falconer [Fal86] proved that the Lebesgue measure of Δ⁡(E)\Delta(E) is positive if dimℋ(E)>d+12\dim_{{\mathcal{H}}}(E)>\frac{d+1}{2}. This exponent was lowered to 139\frac{13}{9} in two dimension by Bourgain [Bou94] and to 43\frac{4}{3} by Wolff [Wol99]. Erdogan [Erd05] established the threshold d2+13\frac{d}{2}+\frac{1}{3} and the subject remained stuck for a while until a flurry of activity in the last couple of years, culminating in the exponent 54\frac{5}{4} by Guth, Iosevich, Ou and Wang [GIOW19] in the plane, the exponent 1.81.8 by Du, Guth, Ou, Wang, Wilson and Zhang [DGOWWZ18] in ℝ3{\mathbb{R}}^{3}, and the exponent d22​d−1\frac{d^{2}}{2d-1} by Du and Zhang [DZ18] in higher dimensions.

It is interesting to note that the 54\frac{5}{4} result in two dimensions is pinned in the sense that the authors prove that there exists x∈Ex\in E such that the Lebesgue measure of Δx​(E)={|x−y|:y∈E}\Delta_{x}(E)=\{|x-y|:y\in E\} is positive. The transition to pinned results was made possible, in part, due to a result by the second author [Liu19] who established the 43\frac{4}{3} pinned threshold in two dimensions.

It is also interesting to formulate an analog of this problem on manifolds. Let MM be a dd-dimensional compact Riemannian manifold without a boundary. Let gg be the associated Riemannian metric, dgd_{g} the induced distance function, and for E⊂ME\subset M define

Δg(E)={dg(x,y):x,y∈E}.\Delta_{g}(E)=\{d_{g}(x,y):x,y\in E\}.

Once again, we ask how large d​i​mℋ​(E)dim_{{\mathcal{H}}}(E) needs to be to ensure that the Lebesgue measure of Δg​(E)\Delta_{g}(E) is positive. The Peres–Schlag machinery [PS00] implies that if d​i​mℋ​(E)>d+12dim_{{\mathcal{H}}}(E)>\frac{d+1}{2}, then there exists x∈Ex\in E such that the Lebesgue measure of the pinned distance set

Δg,x​(E)={dg​(x,y):y∈E}\Delta_{g,x}(E)=\{d_{g}(x,y):y\in E\}

is positive. In fact Peres–Schlag considered very general maps, called generalized projections, that are not even necessarily metrics. Later this problem was studied by Eswarathasan, Iosevich and Taylor [EIT11] (non-pinned version), Iosevich, Taylor and Uriarte-Tuero [ITU16] (pinned version), via Fourier integral operators. Although for technical reasons their general setups look different, on Riemannian metrics their bounds are exactly the same as Peres–Schlag. Recently, by applying local smoothing estimates of Fourier integral operators, Iosevich and Liu [IL19] improve the dimensional exponent on pins (the exceptional sets), while no dimensional exponent better than d+12\frac{d+1}{2} was obtained if pins are required to lie in the given set itself. The main result of this paper is the following.

Theorem 1.1.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a two-dimensional Riemannian manifold without a boundary, equipped with the Riemannian metric gg. Let E⊂ME\subset M be of Hausdorff dimension >54>\frac{5}{4}. Then there exists x∈Ex\in E such that the Lebesgue measure of Δg,x​(E)\Delta_{g,x}(E) is positive.

It is not difficult to see that for any compact two-dimensional Riemannian manifold MM without a boundary and any ϵ>0\epsilon>0 there exists E⊂ME\subset M of Hausdorff dimension 1−ϵ1-\epsilon such that the Lebesgue measure of Δg​(E)\Delta_{g}(E) is zero. This is accomplished by putting a suitable thickened and scaled arithmetic progression on a sufficiently small piece of a geodesic curve. More precisely, one projects the one-dimensional version of the classical Falconer sharpness example (Theorem 2.4 in [Fal86]) onto a small piece of the geodesic. However, the situation in higher dimensions is much more murky. We remind the reader that, in the plane, sharpness examples can be constructed from either arithmetic progressions or lattice points, while in higher dimensions only lattice points would do and the translation invariance of the Euclidean metric is crucial (Theorem 2.4 in [Fal86]). As a general metric may not be translation invariant, now we only have the sharpness of d2\frac{d}{2} when d=2d=2, from “arithmetic progressions” along a geodesic. We suspect that a generic dd-dimensional Riemannian manifold possess a subset EE of Hausdorff dimension d2−ϵ\frac{d}{2}-\epsilon, ϵ\epsilon small, such that the Lebesgue measure of Δg​(E)\Delta_{g}(E) is zero. We shall endeavor to address this question in a sequel.

The proof of Theorem 1.1, just as the proof of its Euclidean predecessor (Theorem 1.1 in [GIOW19]), is based on decoupling theory, a series of Fourier localized LpL^{p} inequalities that underwent rapid development in recent years due to the efforts of Bourgain, Demeter, Guth and others. The application of decoupling theory to the proof of Theorem 1.1 has a variety of new features and complications stemming from the general setup of Riemannian manifolds. In particular, we shall prove a family of decoupling inequalities (Theorem 2.4), which respect a certain microlocal decomposition that naturally generalizes the one used in the Euclidean decoupling theory of Bourgain and Demeter. Similar decompositions were used in the work of Blair and Sogge [BS15] to study concentration of Laplace eigenfunctions. Our work on these variable coefficient decoupling inequalities is inspired by the work of Beltran–Hickman–Sogge [BHS18], where the authors proved certain Wolff-type decoupling inequalities for the variable coefficient wave equation and then used them to obtain sharp local smoothing estimates for the associated Fourier integral operators. Our proof of Theorem 2.4 uses the idea in [BHS18] that one can exploit the multiplicative nature of the decoupling constant to make use of a gain at small scales. We believe that, like the inequalities obtained in [BHS18], the microlocal decoupling inequalities we prove here are interesting in their own right.

This paper is structured as follows. We motivate and set up our main decoupling inequalities in Section 2, with the proof of the key decoupling results carried out in Section 3, parabolic rescaling in Section 4 and the refined decoupling inequality in Section 5. The application of the decoupling technology to distance sets on Riemannian manifolds is set up in Section 6 and carried out in Section 7 and 8. The key analog of Orponen’s radial projection lemma used in [GIOW19] is established in Section 9.

Notation. We shall write A≲BA\lesssim B, if there is an absolute constant CC such that A≤C​BA\leq CB. We shall write A≈BA\approx B, if 910​B≤A≤109​B\frac{9}{10}B\leq A\leq\frac{10}{9}B. We shall use RapDec​(R){\textnormal{RapDec}}(R) to denote a term that is rapidly decaying in R>1R>1, that is, for any N∈ℕN\in{\mathbb{N}}, there exists a constant CNC_{N} such that |RapDec​(R)|≤CN​R−N|{\textnormal{RapDec}}(R)|\leq C_{N}R^{-N}. We shall say that a function is essentially supported in a set EE, if the L∞L^{\infty} norm of the tail outside EE is RapDec​(R){\textnormal{RapDec}}(R) for the underlying parameter RR.

Like its Euclidean counterpart, the oscillatory integral operator SλS_{\lambda}, given by

4. Parabolic rescaling and proof of Lemma 3.3

Parabolic rescaling is already a standard technique in harmonic analysis. Denote by NRN_{R} the R−1R^{-1}-neighborhood of a cap on the hypersurface

{(ω,Σ⁡(ω)):ω∈B1/ρd−1},\{(\omega,\Sigma(\omega)):\omega\in B^{d-1}_{1/\rho}\},

{(ρ​u,ρ2​t):(u,t)∈NR}\{(\rho u,\rho^{2}t):(u,t)\in N_{R}\}

is the (R/ρ2)−1(R/\rho^{2})^{-1}-neighborhood of a cap whose curvature is also ≈1\approx 1. Although our version of the parabolic rescaling lemma is more complicated, this geometric fact will be still used as a key ingredient in the proof. Using parabolic rescaling, we now prove Lemma 3.3.

Let θ0\theta_{0} be the center of the (R/ρ)−1(R/\rho)^{-1}-cap σ∈Sd−1\sigma\in S^{d-1}. Without loss of generality, assume that BRB_{R} is centered at the origin. Consider a finite overlapping collection of curved tubes with length RR and cross-section radius R​ρ−1R\rho^{-1} that are positioned with respect to σ\sigma and cover BRB_{R}. More precisely, decompose [−R,R)d−1[-R,R)^{d-1} into

I=[j1R/ρ,(j1+1)R/ρ)×⋯×[jd−1R/ρ,(jd−1+1)R/ρ),ji∈[−ρ,ρ]∩ℤI=[j_{1}R/\rho,(j_{1}+1)R/\rho)\times\cdots\times[j_{d-1}R/\rho,(j_{d-1}+1)R/\rho),\ j_{i}\in[-\rho,\rho]\cap{\mathbb{Z}}

and then decompose BRB_{R} into

T={x∈BR:u⁡(x,θ0)∈I},T=\{x\in B_{R}:u(x,\theta_{0})\in I\},

where u⁡(x,ξ)u(x,\xi) is as defined in (2.3). It follows that

Fixing a tube TT, after rotation and translation, we may assume the center of σ\sigma is θ0=(0→,1)\theta_{0}=(\vec{0},1), 0→∈ℝd−1\vec{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d-1}, and the central curve passes through the origin. Moreover, in view of (2.4), we also assume that a point xx on the central curve satisfies

4.1. Straightening the Tube.

We would like to perform a parabolic rescaling over the tube TT. However, since our tube TT is defined to be the tubular neighborhood of the central curve, the tangent to the central curve of the tube is changing smoothly along the curve. Thus a simple stretching along fixed orthogonal directions will not always provide desired rescaling for the caps along the curve. To fix this problem, we would like to do a smooth change of variables to Lagrangian coordinates before we do parabolic rescaling. See Figure 2.

To describe this change of variable, first we rescale back to the unit ball, where TT get rescaled back to a tube of length R​λ−1R\lambda^{-1}

5. A Refined Microlocal decoupling Inequality

In this section, we shall use the microlocal decoupling inequalities proved above and the approach in the Euclidean case ([GIOW19]) to obtain further refined decoupling inequalities. In this section, we shall only present the theorem in the two-dimensional case for the critical index p=6p=6 for the sake of simplicity, even though the result can be readily generalized to higher dimensions case for all 2≤p≤2​(d+1)/(d−1)2\leq p\leq 2(d+1)/(d-1) with the same proof. Given 1≤R≤λ1\leq R\leq\lambda, δ>0\delta>0, we shall consider collections of curved tubes 𝕋=∪τ𝕋τ\mathbb{T}=\cup_{\tau}\mathbb{T}_{\tau} associated to the phase function ϕλ\phi^{\lambda}, and arcs τ⊂S1\tau\subset S^{1} of length R−1/2R^{-1/2}. A curved tube TT of length RR and cross-section radius R12+δR^{\frac{1}{2}+\delta} is in 𝕋τ\mathbb{T}_{\tau}, if the central axis of TT is the curve γτt\gamma_{\tau}^{t} given by

γτt={x:−∇yϕλ​(x,(t,0))|∇yϕλ​(x,(t,0))|=center of ​τ},\gamma_{\tau}^{t}=\left\{x:-\frac{\nabla_{y}\phi^{\lambda}(x,(t,0))}{|\nabla_{y}\phi^{\lambda}(x,(t,0))|}{=\text{center of }\tau}\right\},

here tt is chosen from a maximal R12+δR^{\frac{1}{2}+\delta} separated subset of ℝ\mathbb{R}, and θ\theta is the center of τ⊂S1\tau\subset S^{1}. For instance, in the case ϕ=dg\phi=d_{g}, the angle between central geodesic γτ\gamma_{\tau} of TT and the first coordinate axis is θ=\theta= center of τ\tau. We say a function ff is microlocalized to a tube T∈𝕋τT\in\mathbb{T}_{\tau} if ff has microlocal support essentially in Nϕλ,RτN^{\tau}_{\phi^{\lambda},R}, and ff is essentially supported in TT in physical space as well. We remark that the tubes considered in this section is different in size compared to those in the previous section.

Theorem 5.1.

Let 1≤R≤λ1\leq R\leq\lambda. Let ff be a function with microlocal support in Nϕλ,RN_{\phi^{\lambda},R}. Let 𝕋\mathbb{T} be a collection of tubes associated to R−1/2R^{-1/2} caps, and 𝕎⊂𝕋\mathbb{W}\subset\mathbb{T}. Suppose that each T∈𝕎T\in\mathbb{W} is contained in the ball BRB_{R}. Let WW be the cardinality of 𝕎\mathbb{W}. Suppose that

f=∑T∈𝕎fT,f=\sum_{T\in\mathbb{W}}f_{T},

where each fTf_{T} is microlocalized to T∈𝕎T\in\mathbb{W}, and ‖fT‖L6​(ωBR)\|f_{T}\|_{L^{6}(\omega_{B_{R}})} is roughly constant among all T∈𝕎T\in\mathbb{W}. If YY is a union of R12R^{\frac{1}{2}}-cubes in BRB_{R} each of which intersects at most MM tubes T∈𝕎T\in\mathbb{W}. Then

(5.1) ‖f‖L6​(Y)≤Cϵ​Rϵ​(MW)13​(∑T‖fT‖L6​(ωBR)2)12.\|f\|_{L^{6}(Y)}\leq C_{\epsilon}R^{\epsilon}\left(\frac{M}{W}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}(\sum_{T}\|f_{T}\|^{2}_{L^{6}(\omega_{B_{R}})})^{\frac{1}{2}}.

This matches the refined decoupling inequalities appeared in [GIOW19], and the proof is very similar. We include the proof here for the sake of completeness.

Proof.

Like in the proof for the Euclidean case, we shall employ induction on scales via parabolic rescaling. We shall use the microlocal decoupling inequality (2.7) instead of the Bourgain–Demeter decoupling inequality as an input. Since parabolic rescaling is required, we shall prove a stronger theorem which works for all phase function ϕ\phi in our class.

We claim that it is enough to consider that case that ‖f‖Lp​(Q)\|f\|_{L^{p}(Q)} is approximately a constant for all R1/2R^{1/2} cubes Q⊂YQ\subset Y. This technique is called dyadic pigeonholing, which is standard in the study of modern harmonic analysis. We will do this reduction a couple of times in this paper, while details are only provided for this one. More precisely, sort Q⊂YQ\subset Y into different groups

Y1,…,YN,Y≥(N+1),Y_{1},\dots,Y_{N},Y_{\geq(N+1)},

where N=10​d​log⁡RN=10d\,\log R,

Yj={Q⊂Y:2−j+1​‖f‖Lp​(Y)<‖f‖Lp​(Q)≤2−j​‖f‖Lp​(Y)},Y_{j}=\{Q\subset Y:2^{-j+1}\|f\|_{L^{p}(Y)}<\|f\|_{L^{p}(Q)}\leq 2^{-j}\|f\|_{L^{p}(Y)}\},
Y>N={Q⊂Y:‖f‖Lp​(Q)<2−(N+1)​‖f‖Lp​(Y)}.Y_{>N}=\{Q\subset Y:\|f\|_{L^{p}(Q)}<2^{-(N+1)}\|f\|_{L^{p}(Y)}\}.

Since by the trivial estimate ‖f‖Lp​(Y>N)<110​‖f‖Lp​(Y)\|f\|_{L^{p}(Y_{>N})}<\frac{1}{10}\|f\|_{L^{p}(Y)}, we have

‖f‖Lp​(Y)≲∑j=110​d​log⁡R‖f‖Lp​(Yj),\|f\|_{L^{p}(Y)}\lesssim\sum_{j=1}^{10d\,\log R}\|f\|_{L^{p}(Y_{j})},

and therefore there exists j0j_{0} such that

(5.2) ‖f‖Lp​(Y)≲(log⁡R)​‖f‖Lp​(Yj0).\|f\|_{L^{p}(Y)}\lesssim(\log R)\,\|f\|_{L^{p}(Y_{j_{0}})}.

Recall by our definition ‖f‖Lp​(Q)\|f\|_{L^{p}(Q)} is approximately a constant for all R1/2R^{1/2}-cubes in Yj0Y_{j_{0}}. It follows that, if we can prove (5.1) on Yj0Y_{j_{0}}, then (5.1) holds on YY with another log⁡R\log R factor, that can be absorbed by the Cϵ​RϵC_{\epsilon}R^{\epsilon} term.

From now we assume that ‖f‖Lp​(Q)\|f\|_{L^{p}(Q)} is approximately a constant for all R1/2R^{1/2} cubes Q⊂YQ\subset Y.

For each R−1/4R^{-1/4}-cap σ\sigma, we consider the collection of fat tubes in BRB_{R} with length RR and cross-section radius R3/4R^{3/4}, and central axis being γσt\gamma^{t}_{\sigma} for some t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}. Let 𝔽σ\mathbb{F}_{\sigma} be a subcollection of such fat tubes with finite overlaps that covers BRB_{R}. 6. Application to Riemannian distance set

6.1. L2L^{2} method of Mattila–Liu in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}.

In Euclidean spaces, let d⁡(x,y)=dx​(y)=|x−y|d(x,y)=d^{x}(y)=|x-y|, and dimℋ\dim_{\mathcal{H}} denote the Hausdorff dimension. For any compact set E⊂ℝdE\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d}, and any 0<α<dimℋE0<\alpha<\dim_{\mathcal{H}}E, the well known Frostman Lemma (see, e.g. [Mat15]) guarantees that there exists a probability measure μ\mu on EE satisfying

μ⁡(Br​(x))≲rα,∀r>0,x∈ℝd.\mu(B_{r}(x))\lesssim r^{\alpha},\ \forall\,r>0,\,x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}.

Mattila’s approach in [Mat87] is to consider the L2L^{2} boundedness of d∗​(μ×μ),d_{*}(\mu\times\mu), which would imply |Δ⁡(E)|>0|\Delta(E)|>0. This idea was later generalized by Liu [Liu19], who considered the L2L^{2} boundedness of d∗x​(μ)d^{x}_{*}(\mu), which would imply |Δx​(E)|>0.|\Delta_{x}(E)|>0.

Before [GIOW19], the best known dimensional exponent in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} is dimℋE>4/3\dim_{\mathcal{H}}E>4/3, obtained by plugging Wolff’s estimate [Wol99] i nto the approach of Mattila–Liu. The following result shows 4/34/3 cannot be improved via this L2L^{2} method. The construction is based on train-track examples, which is described in details in Section 66 of [GIOW19].

Proposition 6.1 (Guth, Iosevich, Ou, Wang, 2019).

For every 1≤α<4/31\leq\alpha<4/3 and every positive number CC, there is a probability measure μ\mu on B1​(0)B_{1}(0) with the following properties:

  1. (1)

    For any ball Br​(x)B_{r}(x), μ⁡(Br​(x))≲rα\mu(B_{r}(x))\lesssim r^{\alpha}.

  2. (2)

    If d⁡(x,y):=|x−y|d(x,y):=|x-y|, then

    ‖d∗​(μ×μ)‖L2>C.\|d_{*}(\mu\times\mu)\|_{L^{2}}>C.
  3. (3)

    If dx​(y):=|x−y|d^{x}(y):=|x-y|, then for every xx in the support of μ\mu,

    ‖d∗x​(μ)‖L2>C.\|d^{x}_{*}(\mu)\|_{L^{2}}>C.

This shows, to break the 4/34/3 barrier, new ideas beyond the L2L^{2} method above are required. In [GIOW19], authors determine good/bad wave packets, decompose μ=μg​o​o​d+μb​a​d\mu=\mu_{good}+\mu_{bad}, and then show when α>5/4\alpha>5/4 the contribution from μb​a​d\mu_{bad} is negligible and the L2L^{2} method works on μg​o​o​d\mu_{good}. We shall employ the same strategy in the Riemannian case.

6.2. Riemannian distance set and the pruning procedure.

Train track examples can be constructed similarly on manifolds, by forming train-tracks along geodesics in a small enough local chart, and thus the direct analog of Proposition 6.1 holds in the setting of two-dimensional Riemannian manifolds. For this reason we cannot expect to obtain the desired result by estimating the L2L^{2} norm of the distance measure, so we follow [GIOW19] and eliminate the contribution of the “rail tracks” using a suitable pruning procedure. This is where we now turn our attention.

Let (M,g)(M,g) be a Riemannian surface and E⊂ME\subset M be a compact set with positive α\alpha-dimensional Hausdorff measure. Rescaling the metric, if necessary, we can assume that EE is contained in the unit geodesic disk of a coordinate patch of MM, and in this disk, the metric gg is very close to the flat metric. Let E1E_{1} and E2E_{2} be subsets of EE with positive α\alpha-dimensional Hausdorff measure so that the distance from E1E_{1} to E2E_{2} is comparable to 11, and EjE_{j} is supported in some geodesic disk BjB_{j} of radius 1/1001/100. Each EiE_{i} admits a probability measure μi\mu_{i} such that supp⁡μi⊂Ei{\operatorname{supp}}\,\mu_{i}\subset E_{i} and μi​(B⁡(x,r))≲rα.\mu_{i}(B(x,r))\lesssim r^{\alpha}. Here B⁡(x,r)B(x,r) denotes the geodesic disk of radius rr.

Let dgd_{g} be the Riemannian distance function on MM. We define the pushforward measure d∗x​(μ)=(dg)∗x​(μ)d_{*}^{x}(\mu)=(d_{g})_{*}^{x}(\mu) by

∫ℝh⁡(t)​d∗x​(μ)=∫Mh⁡(dg​(x,y))​𝑑μ​(y).\int_{{\mathbb{R}}}h(t)\,d_{*}^{x}(\mu)=\int_{M}h(d_{g}(x,y))\,d\mu(y).

In Euclidean spaces, denote the radial projection centered at y∈ℝdy\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d} by

πy​(x)=x−y|x−y|:ℝd\{y}→Sd−1.\pi^{y}(x)=\frac{x-y}{|x-y|}:{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\backslash\{y\}\rightarrow S^{d-1}.

The following estimate due to Orponen plays an important role in recent work on Falconer distance conjecture [KS19], [GIOW19], [Shm18].

Theorem 9.1 ([Orp19, (3.6)]).

Given compactly supported Borel measures μ\mu, ν\nu in ℝd{\mathbb{R}}^{d} such that supp⁡(μ)∩supp⁡(ν)=∅{\operatorname{supp}}(\mu)\cap{\operatorname{supp}}(\nu)=\emptyset, Is​(μ),It​(ν)<∞I_{s}(\mu),I_{t}(\nu)<\infty, with <2​(d−1)−s<t<d−1<2(d-1)-s<t<d-1. Then for any

1<p≤min⁡{2−td−1,t2​(d−1)−s}1<p\leq\min\{2-\frac{t}{d-1},\frac{t}{2(d-1)-s}\}

we have

(9.1) ∫‖π∗y​(μ)‖Lp​(Sd−1)p​𝑑ν​(y)≲It​(ν)1/2⋅Is​(μ)p/2<∞.\int||\pi^{y}_{*}(\mu)||^{p}_{L^{p}(S^{d-1})}\,d\nu(y)\lesssim I_{t}(\nu)^{1/2}\cdot I_{s}(\mu)^{p/2}<\infty.

In this paper we prove an analog of this result on 22-dimensional Riemannian manifolds, where the radial projection is defined by

πy​(x)=expy−1​x|expy−1​x|∈S1.\pi^{y}(x)=\frac{\exp^{-1}_{y}x}{|\exp^{-1}_{y}x|}\in S^{1}.
Theorem 9.2.

Given compactly supported Borel measures μ\mu, ν\nu on a 22-dimensional Riemannian manifold such that supp⁡(μ)∩supp⁡(ν)=∅{\operatorname{supp}}(\mu)\cap{\operatorname{supp}}(\nu)=\emptyset, Is​(μ),It​(ν)<∞I_{s}(\mu),I_{t}(\nu)<\infty, with 2−s<t<12-s<t<1. Then for any

1<p≤min⁡{2−t,t2−s}1<p\leq\min\{2-t,\frac{t}{2-s}\}

we have

(9.2) ∫‖π∗y​(μ)‖Lp​(S1)p​𝑑ν​(y)≲It​(ν)1/2⋅Is​(μ)p/2<∞.\int||\pi^{y}_{*}(\mu)||^{p}_{L^{p}(S^{1})}\,d\nu(y)\lesssim I_{t}(\nu)^{1/2}\cdot I_{s}(\mu)^{p/2}<\infty.

We believe similar results still hold in higher dimensions. However, in the absence of a good coordinate system in higher dimensions, extra efforts are needed to extend the proof, which would certainly make the argument long and tedious. As we only use radial projections on 22-dimensional manifolds, and this radial projection theorem is not the main contribution of this paper, we choose to only state and prove the 22-dimensional version. In fact, we suspect that in higher dimensions we may need to introduce extra concepts and terminologies from differential geometry that are unfamiliar to many readers of this paper. We plan to address this problem in a sequel.

The proof of Theorem 9.2 is almost the same as Orponen’s. The only difference is, in Euclidean spaces it is reduced to classical estimates on orthogonal projections, while on manifolds we reduce it to estimates of generalized projections due to Peres and Schlag [PS00].

9.1. Orthogonal projections on manifolds

In [PS00], a very broad class of maps, called generalized projections, is studied. We shall show that local orthogonal projections on manifolds lie in this class.

We choose a geodesic γ0\gamma_{0} and work in the Fermi normal coordinates about γ0\gamma_{0}, so that γ0={(x1,0)}\gamma_{0}=\{(x_{1},0)\} in this coordinate system. Then for any u∈ℝu\in{\mathbb{R}} and (cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ)∈S1(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\in S^{1}, denote by πθ​(x)=u\pi_{\theta}(x)=u the “orthogonal projection on manifolds” if there exists t∈ℝt\in{\mathbb{R}} such that exp(u,0)⁡t⁡(cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ)=x\exp_{(u,0)}t(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)=x. This projection map is always well-defined as long as we work within a small enough local chart. We will also assume that x2x_{2} is bounded away from 00. Note that in this case we must have

(cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ)=−∇ydg​(x,(πθ​(x),0))|∇ydg​(x,(πθ​(x),0))|.(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)=-\dfrac{\nabla_{y}{d_{g}(x,(\pi_{\theta}(x),0))}}{|\nabla_{y}{d_{g}(x,(\pi_{\theta}(x),0))}|}.

Since we are working in the Fermi coordinates about γ0={(x1,0)}\gamma_{0}=\{(x_{1},0)\}, we have that gi​j​(u,0)=δi​jg_{ij}(u,0)=\delta_{ij}, where (gi​j)(g_{ij}) denotes the metric matrix, and thus ∇ydg​(x,(u,0))\nabla_{y}{d_{g}(x,(u,0))} must be a unit vector. Therefore

(9.3) (ω→⋅∇x)​∇ydg​(x,(u,0))⟂∇ydg​(x,(u,0)),∀ω→∈S1(\vec{\omega}\cdot\nabla_{x})\nabla_{y}d_{g}(x,(u,0))\perp\nabla_{y}d_{g}(x,(u,0)),\ \forall\,\vec{\omega}\in S^{1}

and by our definition of πθ\pi_{\theta} we have

(9.4) (cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ)=−∇ydg​(x,(πθ​(x),0)).(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)=-\nabla_{y}{d_{g}(x,(\pi_{\theta}(x),0))}.

The formula (9.4) significantly simplifies our computations. Unfortunately, a higher dimensional analog is not generally available.

Since ω→\vec{\omega} is arbitrary in (9.3), we see that (cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ)(\cos\theta,\sin\theta) must be contained in the kernel of the rank 1 matrix Aθ:=∇x​y2dg​(x,(πθ​(x),0))A_{\theta}:=\nabla^{2}_{xy}d_{g}(x,(\pi_{\theta}(x),0)), that is

(9.5) Aθ⋅(cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ)T=(0,0)T.A_{\theta}\cdot(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)^{T}=(0,0)^{T}.

If we fix xx, take ∂θ\partial_{\theta} on both sides of (9.5), we have

(9.6) ∂θAθ⋅(cosθ,sinθ)T=−Aθ⋅(−sinθ,cosθ)T,\partial_{\theta}A_{\theta}\cdot(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)^{T}=-A_{\theta}\cdot(-\sin\theta,\cos\theta)^{T},

Since AθA_{\theta} has rank 1 and (cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ)T(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)^{T} is in its kernel, both sides of (9.6) have norm ≳1\gtrsim 1.

To apply estimates in [PS00], we need to check the regularity condition and the transversality condition. From the local smoothness of the exponential map one concludes that all derivatives of πθ​(x)\pi_{\theta}(x) are bounded, so the regularity condition is satisfied. It remains to check the transversality condition on πθ\pi_{\theta}, namely

(9.7) |ω→⋅∇xπθ|≪1⟹|∂θ(ω→⋅∇xπθ)|≳1,∀ω→∈S1.|\vec{\omega}\cdot\nabla_{x}\pi_{\theta}|\ll 1\implies|\partial_{\theta}(\vec{\omega}\cdot\nabla_{x}\pi_{\theta})|\gtrsim 1,\ \forall\,\vec{\omega}\in S^{1}.

Notice these conditions are obvious under the Euclidean metric where πθ​(x)=x1+x2​cot⁡θ\pi_{\theta}(x)=x_{1}+x_{2}\cot\theta.

By differentiating both sides of (9.4) in θ\theta, one can see

|∂y1∇ydg|,|∂θπθ|≳1.|\partial_{y_{1}}\nabla_{y}d_{g}|,|\partial_{\theta}\pi_{\theta}|\gtrsim 1.

Also we can take ∇x\nabla_{x} on both sides of (9.4) to have

(9.8) Aθ+∂y1∇ydg​(x,(πθ​(x),0))T⋅∇xπθ​(x)=0.A_{\theta}+\partial_{y_{1}}\nabla_{y}d_{g}(x,(\pi_{\theta}(x),0))^{T}\cdot\nabla_{x}\pi_{\theta}(x)=0.

As AθA_{\theta} is not a 00 matrix, one concludes |∇xπθ|≳1|\nabla_{x}\pi_{\theta}|\gtrsim 1. If we multiply both sides of (9.8) by (cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ)T(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)^{T} from the right, then by (9.5) and |∂y1∇ydg|≳1|\partial_{y_{1}}\nabla_{y}d_{g}|\gtrsim 1, it follows that ∇xπθ⋅(cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ)=0\nabla_{x}\pi_{\theta}\cdot(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)=0. Therefore

(9.9) |ω→⋅∇xπθ|≪1⟹|ω→−(cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ)|≪1.|\vec{\omega}\cdot\nabla_{x}\pi_{\theta}|\ll 1\implies|\vec{\omega}-(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)|\ll 1.

Now we fix xx and take ∂θ\partial_{\theta} on both sides of (9.8) to get

(9.10) ∂θAθ+(∂θπθ)​(∂y12∇ydg)T⋅(∇xπθ)+(∂y1∇ydg)T⋅(∂θ∇xπθ)=0.\partial_{\theta}A_{\theta}+(\partial_{\theta}\pi_{\theta})(\partial^{2}_{y_{1}}\nabla_{y}d_{g})^{T}\cdot(\nabla_{x}\pi_{\theta})+(\partial_{y_{1}}\nabla_{y}d_{g})^{T}\cdot(\partial_{\theta}\nabla_{x}\pi_{\theta})=0.

If we multiply it by ω→T\vec{\omega}^{T} from the right, then we have

(9.11) ∂θAθ⋅ω→T+(∂θπθ)​(ω→⋅∇xπθ)​(∂y12∇ydg)T+(∂θ(ω→⋅∇xπθ))​(∂y1∇ydg)T=0.\partial_{\theta}A_{\theta}\cdot\vec{\omega}^{T}+(\partial_{\theta}\pi_{\theta})(\vec{\omega}\cdot\nabla_{x}\pi_{\theta})(\partial^{2}_{y_{1}}\nabla_{y}d_{g})^{T}+(\partial_{\theta}(\vec{\omega}\cdot\nabla_{x}\pi_{\theta}))(\partial_{y_{1}}\nabla_{y}d_{g})^{T}=0.

By (9.9), if |ω→⋅∇xπθ|≪1|\vec{\omega}\cdot\nabla_{x}\pi_{\theta}|\ll 1 then ω→\vec{\omega} is close to (cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ)(\cos\theta,\sin\theta). Therefore the first term has norm about 1 by (9.6). Hence (9.7) holds and the transversality condition is checked.

With the regularity condition and the transversality condition, it is known that (see [PS00], or [Mat15, Chapter 18])

In particular, since by Hölder

9.2. Proof of Theorem 9.2

We follow Orponen’s argument in [Orp19, Section 3]. We may assume μ,ν∈C0∞\mu,\nu\in C_{0}^{\infty}, then the general case follows by a standard limit argument (see [Orp19] for details).

The first step is to reduce radial projections to orthogonal projections: for any p>0p>0,

(9.14) ∫‖π∗y​(μ)‖Lp​(S1)p​𝑑ν​(y)≈∬|(πθ)∗​μ​(u)|p​(πθ)∗​ν​(u)​𝑑u​ℋ1​(θ).\int||\pi^{y}_{*}(\mu)||^{p}_{L^{p}(S^{1})}\,d\nu(y)\approx\iint|(\pi_{\theta})_{*}\mu(u)|^{p}(\pi_{\theta})_{*}\nu(u)\,du\,\mathcal{H}^{1}(\theta).

where the implicit constant only depends on d​i​s​t​(supp⁡(μ),supp⁡(ν))dist({\operatorname{supp}}(\mu),{\operatorname{supp}}(\nu)).

To see this, for any f∈C⁡(S1)f\in C(S^{1}),

Since dist​(x,y)≈1\text{dist}(x,y)\approx 1, by polar coordinates in Ty​MT_{y}M it approximately equals

∫S1f⁡(e)​∫μ⁡(expy⁡t​e)​𝑑t​d​ℋ1​(e).\int_{S^{1}}f(e)\int\mu(\exp_{y}te)\,dt\,d\mathcal{H}^{1}(e).

where θ⁡(⋅,⋅)\theta({}\cdot{},{}\cdot{}) is as defined in (2.4).

Since the exponential map is a local diffeomorphism on the tangent bundle, the map that sends y,ey,e to u=πθ⁡(y,e),θ=θ⁡(y,e)u=\pi_{\theta(y,e)},\theta=\theta(y,e) is differentiable, with Jacobian ≈1\approx 1. Therefore

Now it suffices to consider the right-hand side of (9.14). It is known that (see [Orp19, Lemma 3.4]) if 2−s+ϵ∈(0,1)2-s+\epsilon\in(0,1), then
